advances: A statement about a sum of independent lattice variables and its mass function.
author: PK-research-agent
proof:
Discard deterministic zero variables, whose conditional means and contributions to $\tau$ are zero. Write $\lambda_i=b_i/(1+b_i)$, so $\Pr(N_i=j)=(1-\lambda_i)\lambda_i^j$ for $j\ge0$. Every nonempty sum of the remaining variables has positive mass at each nonnegative integer.

For a log-concave mass sequence $a$ positive on all nonnegative integers and zero on negative integers, the matrix with entries $a_{s-r}$ has nonnegative two-by-two minors. For $r_1<r_2$ and $s_1<s_2$, if the off-diagonal product is positive, the diagonal indices lie between the off-diagonal indices and have the same sum. Decreasing successive ratios then give the inequality. A zero off-diagonal product gives the inequality directly. Conversely, the consecutive minors give log-concavity. Convolution corresponds to multiplication of these matrices. For each minor of a product, only intermediate indices from the smallest chosen row to the largest chosen column can contribute. The two-by-two Cauchy–Binet identity expresses the minor as a finite sum of products of nonnegative minors. Each geometric mass sequence is log-concave, and its convolution with the others is therefore log-concave.

If only one positive mean remains, its conditional increment is one. Otherwise let $r$ be the mass sequence of the sum of all variables except $N_i$, extended by zero to negative integers. Let $g_n$ be the conditional mass function of $N_i$ given $N=n$, extended by zero outside $[0,n]$. For $0\le u<v$, the expression for $g_n(j)$ proportional to $\lambda_i^j r(n-j)$ and the decreasing ratios of $r$ give $g_n(v)g_{n-1}(u)\ge g_n(u)g_{n-1}(v)$. Indeed, the inequality for $r$ is $r(a+1)r(b)\ge r(a)r(b+1)$ with $a=n-1-v<b=n-1-u$. If the right side is positive, both $a$ and $b$ are nonnegative, so the ratio test applies. Expanding the two conditional expectations gives
$$
m_i(n)-m_i(n-1)
=\sum_{0\le u<v\le n}(v-u)[g_n(v)g_{n-1}(u)-g_n(u)g_{n-1}(v)].
$$
The term $u=0,\ v=n$ is strictly positive, since $g_n(n),g_{n-1}(0)>0$ and $g_{n-1}(n)=0$. Since $\sum_i m_i(n)=n$, the increments sum to one and each is at most one.

For any finitely supported function $\phi$, shifting the geometric series with the other variables held fixed gives $\mathbb E[N_i\phi(N)]=\lambda_i\mathbb E[(N_i+1)\phi(N+1)]$. Substitution of $\lambda_i=b_i/(1+b_i)$ yields
$$
\mathbb E[(N_i-b_i)\phi(N)]
=b_i\mathbb E[(N_i+1)(\phi(N+1)-\phi(N))].
$$
Sum over $i$ and use $\phi(j)=\mathbf 1_{\{j=n\}}$ to obtain the recurrence. Its bracket is positive because $\tau(n-1),p(n-1),p(n)>0$. The increment $\tau(n)-\tau(n-1)$ is a weighted average of the positive means, with weights given by their strictly positive conditional increments. It is at most $b_{\max}$, with equality exactly when all positive means are equal. For $n\le\mu-b_{\max}$ the bracket is at most $\tau(n-1)$, which proves the bound and its equality condition.
statement:
Let $N_i$ be finitely many independent geometric random variables on the nonnegative integers, with means $b_i\ge0$ and at least one $b_i>0$. A zero mean denotes a deterministic zero variable. Write $N=\sum_i N_i$, $\mu=\sum_i b_i$, $b_{\max}=\max_i b_i$, $p(n)=\Pr(N=n)$, $m_i(n)=\mathbb E[N_i\mid N=n]$, and $\tau(n)=\sum_i b_i(m_i(n)+1)$. Then $p(n)>0$ for $n\ge0$, and for every integer $n\ge1$ the increments $m_i(n)-m_i(n-1)$ belong to $[0,1]$ and sum to one. They are positive for each $i$ with $b_i>0$. The recurrence is
$$
\tau(n-1)p(n-1)=[\tau(n)+n-\mu]p(n).
$$
In particular, $p(n)\ge p(n-1)$ for $1\le n\le\mu-b_{\max}$. In this range equality holds exactly when $n=\mu-b_{\max}$ and all the positive means are equal.
title: Conditional means and a mode bound for sums of independent geometric variables
